title: A Simple Trick That Makes Modeling Unforgettable ettable/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin shares a specific modeling technique designed to make routines and expectations stick in students' memories: inserting a deliberately insignificant, silly step into an otherwise practical demonstration. Whether it's a dance move, an animal sound, or a funny phrase, this extraneous detail has no functional purpose but causes students to pay closer attention and visualize the sequence more vividly, which he argues is the essential mechanism behind effective modeling. He illustrates the concept with a personal story about a poster reading 'Work Like A Champion Today' that doubled as a physical touchstone students tapped each morning, transforming an ordinary transition into a meaningful ritual tied to a commitment to excellence. Linsin emphasizes that the technique doesn't need lofty symbolism to work — it can simply add novelty and fun — but either way, it strengthens the memorability and effectiveness of routines like turning in work or transitioning between subjects.
points: Adding a deliberately silly, purposeless step to modeling makes routines significantly more memorable for students.
The technique works because it draws heightened attention and strengthens students' visualization of the steps involved.
Visualization is central to effective modeling — students who can picture themselves succeeding are more likely to do so.
A physical touchstone, like a poster students tap, can transform a mundane transition into a meaningful ritual.
The added step doesn't need deep symbolism; novelty and fun alone can boost engagement and follow-through.
quotes: The way it works is that somewhere in the midst of your modeling exercise—regardless of what it is—you’re going to add an insignificant detail. That’s right. You’re going to add a step that has no purpose whatsoever.
The reason the strategy works is because it causes students to pay closer attention to you. It draws them into a visualization of the steps you want them to take.
If your students are able to see themselves completing the steps successfully, then that’s what they’ll do—no matter how challenging the task.

I had a small round target just below the inscription that each student would tap on their way in. It was a touchstone for them that would immediately shift their focus from life outside of the classroom to the expectations and responsibilities within.
It can be used simply as a small and simple way to get your students to sit up a little higher, smile a little broader, and engage a little deeper.
It will make your modeling more effective and your classroom more fun.
